maths.problem: In the Rice Galaxy experiment, Meenakshi counted 24 grains along the thread towards the middle and 8 grains along the thread away from the middle. How many times as many grains were towards the middle?
maths.explain: 24 divided by 8 is 3. So there were 3 times as many grains towards the middle. This shows the paper Sun is not in the middle.
maths.context: In the Rice Galaxy experiment, rice grains spread on a big paper circle stand for the stars of the Milky Way. A paper Sun sits halfway between the middle and the edge, and the child counts grains along threads in different directions.
maths.why_maths: Dividing one count by the other tells how much bigger it is, which shows how far off-centre the Sun is.

maths.problem: In the Pinhole Galaxy experiment, Kavya's 2 millimetre pair became one light at 4 steps, and her 4 millimetre pair at 8 steps. Guess at how many steps her 6 millimetre pair will become one light. Explain your guess.
maths.explain: When the gap doubled from 2 to 4 millimetres, the steps doubled from 4 to 8. So each millimetre of gap adds about 2 steps. 6 millimetres times 2 is 12 steps.
maths.context: In the Pinhole Galaxy experiment, a card with pairs of needle holes is lit from behind by a torch in a dark room. The child walks back step by step until each pair of lights looks like one light.
maths.why_maths: Spotting the pattern in your results lets you predict a result before you test it.

maths.problem: In the Katori of Rice challenge, one teaspoon held 300 grains, and the katori held 12 teaspoons. About how many grains were in the katori?
maths.explain: 12 times 300 is 3,600. This is an estimate, because each teaspoon holds a slightly different number.
maths.context: In the Katori of Rice challenge, the child counts the grains in one teaspoon, then counts how many teaspoons fill a katori.
maths.why_maths: Multiplying a small count is how astronomers estimate the number of stars without counting every one.

maths.problem: The Sun takes about 230 million years to go once round the galaxy. The Earth is about 4,600 million years old. About how many times has the Earth gone round the galaxy with the Sun?
maths.explain: 230 times 20 is 4,600. So in 4,600 million years the Sun and Earth have gone round about 20 times.
maths.why_maths: Comparing two huge times by dividing tells how many galaxy trips the Earth has made.

maths.problem: The Milky Way is about 100,000 light-years across and about 1,000 light-years thick. How many times wider is it than it is thick? A dosa is 20 centimetres across. How thick would it be if it were as flat as the Milky Way?
maths.answer: 100 times wider. The dosa would be 2 millimetres thick.
maths.explain: 100,000 divided by 1,000 is 100. 20 centimetres is 200 millimetres. 200 divided by 100 is 2 millimetres, about as thin as a real thin dosa.
maths.why_maths: Turning the galaxy's huge sizes into the size of a dosa shows just how flat it is.

maths.problem: In the Rice Galaxy experiment, Lakshmi's counts with the long thread were: towards the middle 22, away 7, left side 14, right side 13. Draw a bar chart of her counts. Which bar is tallest, and what does it tell you?
maths.answer: The bar for 'towards the middle' is tallest, at 22. It shows the most stars lie in that direction, so that is where the middle of the galaxy is.
maths.explain: Draw four bars: 22, 7, 14 and 13. The two side bars are nearly the same, because the middle is neither left nor right.
maths.context: In the Rice Galaxy experiment, rice grains spread on a big paper circle stand for the stars of the Milky Way. A paper Sun sits halfway between the middle and the edge, and the child counts grains along threads in different directions.
maths.why_maths: A bar chart shows at a glance which direction has the most stars.

roots.context: We have been learning that the Milky Way is a galaxy of billions of stars, which our eyes see as one pale glow. Now we ask what that tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: Up close, your pinholes were separate lights, and from across the room they made one soft glow. The holes had not changed. Your eyes could no longer tell them apart. The Milky Way's pale band is billions of stars, blurred into one glow by distance in this way.
deep_truth.habit: We take what we see as one thing to be one thing: a cloud, a smudge, a glow. Whether we see one or many often depends on how far away we are and how fine our eyes are.
deep_truth.evidence: In the Pinhole Galaxy experiment, the bunch of holes looked like one fuzzy light from far away and like separate points up close. Galileo's telescope did the same to the Milky Way in 1610.

three.who_am_i: Your body is made of about 30 trillion cells, more than the stars in the Milky Way. From across the room, you look like one person.
three.what_is_life: A dung beetle must roll their ball of dung away in a straight line, before other beetles steal it. On moonless nights, they steer by the bright band of the Milky Way.
three.what_is_this_world: The Sun is one star in a galaxy of billions, and our galaxy is one of hundreds of billions. All the stars we can see by eye belong to just one of them.

roots.thread: A galaxy is many and one at the same time. It is billions of separate suns, each with its own light. Gravity holds them all, so they all go round one centre together. From far away their lights join into one glow. Each star is fully itself, and each is also part of something bigger that it cannot leave.

teachings.source: Milindapanha (The Questions of King Milinda), Book 2, the simile of the chariot
teachings.teaching: King Milinda asks the monk Nagasena what a chariot is. Is it the wheels, the axle or the pole? None of them alone. 'Chariot' is the name we give to all the parts together.
teachings.link: 'Milky Way' is the name we give to billions of stars, gas and dust together. The glow you see is not any one star, and it is not something extra on top of them.

teachings.teaching: If the light of a thousand suns blazed out together in the sky, it might be like the splendour of that great being.
teachings.link: The pale band of the Milky Way really is the light of countless suns shining together. Each is too far and too faint to see alone. Together they make a glow you can see from a dark hill.

science.text: There are hundreds of billions of galaxies in the part of the universe we can see. The exact number is still argued about.
Most of the matter holding galaxies together seems to be dark matter that gives out no light. Nobody has yet found what it is made of.

other_view.view: A galaxy is only a word for stars that gravity keeps near each other. Only the stars, the gas and the dust are real things. Calling it 'one' is just a handy way of speaking, the way we call many trees a forest.

practice.title: Many lights, one glow
practice.say: Let's sit quietly and look at the lights of the street or the buildings outside. Look at one light far away. Now half close your eyes. Do the lights start to blur together? Open them wide again. Now close your eyes and breathe slowly six times. Feel your whole body breathing as one. Your body is made of trillions of tiny cells, each one alive. Open your eyes slowly.
practice.kid: Look at the far lights outside. Half close your eyes. Do they blur? Now close your eyes. Breathe slowly six times. Your body is trillions of cells, breathing as one.

ask: Is the Milky Way one thing or billions of things? Can it be both?
When the pinhole lights blurred into one glow, was the glow in the card or in your eyes?
Could your cells feel as if they each live alone, the way each star shines alone?
roots.art: A child on a rooftop looking up at the pale band of the Milky Way. In a circle, the band zoomed in to show countless separate stars. In another circle, the child's hand zoomed in to show countless separate cells.

playtest: Every experiment, activity, game, project and challenge was walked through as if in a city flat, with the materials listed. Pinhole card: holes made with a needle tip are well under a millimetre wide, so pairs 2, 4 and 6 millimetres apart stay separate up close. Our eyes can split two points only when their gap looks bigger than about one sixtieth of a degree, and bright points in the dark blur sooner. So a 2 millimetre pair should join within a few metres, and the 6 millimetre pair may stay two across a small flat. The step tells the parent that 'still two at the far wall' is a result too, and the pattern, not the number, is what matters. Rice galaxy: one heaped tablespoon of raw rice is several hundred grains, so a 50 centimetre circle gives roughly 20 grains along the thread towards the middle and under 10 away from it, a clear difference to count. The night activity is outside the spine, because clouds, the season and city light decide what can be seen.

how_we_found_out.story: A hundred years ago, most astronomers thought the Milky Way was the whole universe. Telescopes showed faint spiral clouds, called nebulae. Many thought they were clouds of gas inside our galaxy. Others said they were separate galaxies, far outside. Nobody could measure how far away they were. The answer came from Henrietta Leavitt, who worked at Harvard College Observatory studying photographs of stars. She looked at stars that grow brighter and dimmer again and again, called Cepheids. In 1912 she showed that the brighter a Cepheid really is, the more slowly it pulses. So a Cepheid's pulse tells how bright it really is, and how faint it looks tells how far away it is. In October 1923, Edwin Hubble photographed the Andromeda nebula with the big telescope on Mount Wilson in California and found a Cepheid in it. Using Leavitt's rule, he worked out that it was nearly a million light-years away, far outside the Milky Way. Today we know Andromeda is about 2 and a half million light-years away. Andromeda was a whole galaxy, and the Milky Way was one of many. Leavitt had died in 1921, so she never knew.
how_we_found_out.who: Henrietta Swan Leavitt, an American astronomer at Harvard College Observatory, and Edwin Hubble, an American astronomer at Mount Wilson Observatory
how_we_found_out.when: 1912 (Leavitt's rule) and 1923 (Hubble's Cepheid in Andromeda), announced in 1925
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: Most astronomers thought the Milky Way was the whole universe and the spiral nebulae were clouds inside it. Hubble used Leavitt's pulsing stars to show that Andromeda is far outside the Milky Way, a galaxy of its own.
